3.title: Letters of Recommendation, the New Covenant, and the Unveiled Face
3.overview:
Chapter 3 addresses the question of credentials and letters of recommendation, and immediately turns it into a sustained theological meditation on the new covenant. Paul’s opponents apparently carried letters of recommendation from someone — possibly Jerusalem, possibly the “super-apostles.” Paul refuses to play that game: his letter of recommendation is the Corinthian church itself, written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts. This triggers an extended comparison between the old covenant (the ministry of Moses, the tablets of stone, the fading glory) and the new covenant (the ministry of the Spirit, the surpassing glory, the unveiled face).

The comparison is not a rejection of Moses — Paul repeatedly insists that the old covenant had real glory. But the glory was fading (katargoumenon), and it required a veil over Moses’s face so that the Israelites could not see the glory’s end. The veil is now interpreted allegorically by Paul: the same veil lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without seeing Christ. When one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. And then Paul reaches the climax of the chapter: we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another — for this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Ministers of the New Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question of letters of recommendation (v. 1, systatikōn epistolōn) was live in the early church: itinerant teachers and apostles carried written commendations from churches or leaders to vouch for their authenticity (cf. Acts 18:27; Rom. 16:1). Paul’s opponents apparently had such letters, and wanted letters from Corinth to carry onward; Paul, who founded the Corinthian church himself, needs none. They are his letter.

But Paul immediately spiritualises and deepens the image (vv. 2–3): the Corinthians are a letter of Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts. The echo of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26–27 is explicit — the promised new covenant, in which God’s law would be written on hearts rather than stone, is being fulfilled in the transformation of the Corinthians.

Verse 4 names the settled confidence this gives him, and locates it carefully: it is held “through Christ toward God,” not in himself and not against his rivals. Verse 5 then guards it from any hearing as self-assurance, and answers the question left hanging at 2:16 — who is sufficient for these things? Nobody is. “Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God, who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant” (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between letter and Spirit (v. 6) — “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” — is one of the most misunderstood phrases in Paul. It does not mean that the written word of Scripture is deadly and only spiritual illumination gives life (a Gnostic-leaning interpretation). In context, “the letter” (to gramma) refers specifically to the Mosaic law written on stone — the external commandment that makes demands it cannot empower fulfilling, that reveals sin it cannot remove. The Spirit gives life by doing what the letter could not: writing the law on the heart, enabling obedience from the inside. This is the Jeremiah 31/Ezekiel 36 promise in Paul’s theological shorthand.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation that prides itself on doctrinal correctness — its members can pass any biblical literacy test, articulate the five points of Calvinism, and explain every Confession — but whose relational life is cold and whose evangelistic impact is minimal. The letter/Spirit contrast is not a critique of doctrine or written Scripture; it is a diagnosis of the difference between external knowledge of the truth and inward transformation by it. The new covenant minister’s goal is not to fill heads but to be the instrument through whom the Spirit writes on hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?

Paul has just said that he speaks as a man commissioned by God, in the sight of God. He hears at once how that could be taken, and he says so: is this Paul recommending himself again?

The question is not paranoid. It is what his opponents had been saying. The word again tells us the charge was already in circulation — that his letters were a long exercise in self-promotion, that a man who really had God’s authority would not need to keep asserting it.

Behind the second question lies a real first-century practice worth knowing about. Travel was dangerous, communication slow, and a stranger arriving in a city claiming to teach in the name of Christ could be anyone. So churches wrote letters of recommendation for those they sent. Luke records one: when Apollos wanted to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him (Acts 18:27). Paul himself commends Phoebe to the Romans in exactly this way (Rom. 16:1–2). There is nothing wrong with the practice and Paul does not attack it.

What he attacks is what it had become in Corinth. His rivals had arrived carrying impressive documents from somewhere, and the documents had done their work. Notice the second half of his question: or from you? They wanted letters from Corinth as well as to it — the endorsement of a well-known church to carry to the next town. The credential had become a currency.

That is a shape worth recognising, because it has not gone away. The modern equivalents are easy to name: the conference platform, the endorsement on a book jacket, the size of a following, the association with a bigger name. None of these is wrong in itself, and all of them can be made to do the job a life is supposed to do. The question is only ever whether the credential is describing something real or standing in for it.

There is a genuine tension here that Paul does not dodge and neither should we. He is about to spend eleven chapters defending himself, and he knows it. He calls it foolishness when he gets there. So when is speaking about your own ministry legitimate?

The answer this chapter gives is that it is legitimate when the people you serve are being taken from you, and illegitimate when your own standing is what is at stake. Paul is not protecting a career. He is protecting a church from teachers who will damage it, and the only thing standing between them is his credibility. A man who defends himself for his own sake is building a reputation; a man who defends himself because his people are in danger is doing something else entirely, and the difference is usually visible in whether he enjoys it. Paul plainly does not.

And his answer, when it comes in the next verse, is not another document. It is them.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

Asked for his credentials, Paul points at the people who are asking.

Stand in the room and feel the force of it. They wanted parchment. He tells them that the document is the congregation itself — the former idolaters, the reformed swindlers, the slaves and freedmen sitting in that hall who a few years earlier had never heard the name of Jesus. That is the letter. It is not filed; it walks around Corinth doing business, and the whole city can read it.

Two phrases repay slowing down.

Written on our hearts. Before they are a public document they are a private one, carried inside him. This is a man who has been criticised, humiliated and dismissed by these people, and he says they are written on his heart. He cannot get them out. Anyone who has loved a difficult congregation, or a difficult child, knows the feeling of carrying people who have cost you a great deal.

A letter from Christ delivered by us. Note the correction. In verse 2 they are Paul’s letter; here they are Christ’s, and Paul is downgraded to the courier. He did not write them. He carried them. Every faithful minister eventually discovers this — that he is the postman, not the author, and that the change he sees in people was not produced by his own hand.

Then the two great contrasts, and they are not decorative. Paul is quoting the Old Testament without naming it.

Not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. Ink sits on a surface. It can be scraped off a papyrus with a knife, which is exactly how ancient documents were reused. Something written with the Spirit is not applied to the outside of a person.

Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts. Now the reference is unmistakable. Stone tablets were what Moses carried down Sinai. And centuries later God had promised through Jeremiah, to a nation that had comprehensively failed to keep what was on them: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33). Ezekiel put it more bluntly still: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26).

Paul’s claim is enormous. He is saying that the thing the prophets promised for a far-off day has happened, and that the evidence is sitting in front of him in a difficult church in a Greek port. The new covenant is not a doctrine he is teaching. It is a group of people he is pointing at.

Which raises the question worth carrying out of this passage. Stone can be inscribed and remain stone; that is the whole tragedy of the old covenant. So what has actually been written on you? Not what you can recite — the law on stone could be recited perfectly by people it never changed. The test is whether anything has moved inward: whether you have come to want what you used to merely comply with. That shift is not something a person performs on himself. It is what the Spirit of the living God does with a heart, and it is the only credential any church has ever really had.

verseByVerse.quote: Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,

Paul has just made a very large claim, and he immediately guards it from being heard as self-assurance.

The confidence is real — the word is pepoithēsis, settled trust, the state of a man who is not looking over his shoulder. But look where it is anchored: through Christ toward God. It travels along one route and faces in one direction. It is not confidence in himself measured against his rivals. It is confidence before God, and the way to it goes through Christ.

Then, in case anyone should still mishear, verse 5 takes it apart with almost painful precision. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us. Not merely insufficient for the big things; insufficient to claim anything as originating in himself.

This is the answer to the question he left hanging at the end of chapter 2 — who is sufficient for these things? — and it has taken him nine verses to give it. The answer is nobody. And then: our sufficiency is from God.

The word running through both verses is hikanos and its noun hikanotēs: adequate, competent, up to the job. It is a word with a history. When God met Moses at the bush and told him to go to Pharaoh, Moses said, Who am I that I should go? When God called Jeremiah, he said, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth. When Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple he said, Woe is me, for I am lost. Every one of them was right. Not one of them was adequate. God’s answer in each case was never to argue the point; it was to supply what was missing.

So here is a test, and it cuts both ways. Ask yourself which of these two sentences you actually live in: I can do this, or I cannot do this and it is going to be done anyway. The first sounds like faith and is usually self-reliance in good clothes. The second sounds like defeat and is where God does most of his work.

And there is a real comfort in it for anyone who has ever backed away from something because they did not feel up to it — the class they were asked to teach, the neighbour they were meant to speak to, the parent they have to care for, the marriage they no longer know how to mend. The feeling of inadequacy is not a verdict. It is accurate. Paul felt it and said so in writing. What he learned is that adequacy was never the entry requirement, because it was never going to be supplied from inside him.

Notice, finally, the direction of the preposition: our sufficiency is from God — it comes out of him and arrives in us. It is not that God helps a competent man do a little more than he could alone. The competence itself is on loan, issued daily, and never becomes the property of the person using it. That is why Paul can be bold in the next paragraph and humble in this one at the same time. Both are the same fact seen from two ends.

verseByVerse.quote: who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Two enormous things are in this verse: what a minister of the new covenant is, and one of the most abused sentences in the whole Bible.

Take the abuse first, because it has done real damage. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life has been used for centuries to mean that careful attention to the text of Scripture is deadening, while a spiritual impression is where the life is. On that reading, the man who studies the words is quenching the Spirit, and the man who bypasses them is free. Whole movements have been built on it.

It cannot mean that, and the context makes it plain. Look at what the two words are set against in the same sentence: not text against feeling, but the letter against a new covenant. And in the very next verse Paul defines his terms: the ministry of death was carved in letters on stone. The letter is the law of Moses, inscribed on tablets, standing outside a person and telling him what to do.

So why does it kill? Not because it is bad. Paul says elsewhere that the law is holy and righteous and good (Rom. 7:12). It kills because of what it can and cannot do. It can tell you the standard with perfect accuracy; it cannot give you the least power to meet it. A speed limit painted on a road has never slowed a single car by itself. A doctor’s diagnosis has never cured anyone. The law describes the disease with total precision and hands you no medicine — and a diagnosis with no cure is a death sentence read aloud.

And the Spirit gives life by doing the one thing the stone could never do: writing the command inside, on a heart that has been made new, so that obedience comes out rather than being demanded in.

Which means the popular misuse of this verse gets it exactly backwards. Ignoring the words of Scripture is not walking in the Spirit; the Spirit is the one who inspired them. The real warning here is aimed somewhere much closer to home — at the person who knows the Bible thoroughly, keeps the rules scrupulously, and has never been changed by any of it. That is life under the letter, and it can be conducted with a well-marked Bible.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in a quiet way. When you obey God this week, where does it come from? Is it a wall you keep running into, or a direction you actually want to go? Both people do the same thing on Sunday. Only one of them has had anything written on the inside.

And notice what Paul says he has been made sufficient to be: a minister of a new covenant. Not a better teacher of the old one. Something the prophets promised and never saw. When the Lord sat down with his disciples the night before he died and lifted the cup, he said this cup is the new covenant in my blood (Lk. 22:20). The covenant Jeremiah waited for was not inaugurated with tablets on a mountain but with a body given and blood poured out. What the stone could only require, he came and supplied, and then wrote it into his people by his Spirit. The letter could kill; it took the death of the Lawgiver’s Son to make anything alive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–18 — The Fading Glory and the Surpassing Glory; the Unveiled Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul develops an extended comparison between the Mosaic ministry (the ministry of death, the ministry of condemnation) and the new covenant ministry (the ministry of the Spirit, the ministry of righteousness). He is careful not to denigrate the Mosaic covenant: it had real glory — Moses’s face shone so brightly after Sinai that the Israelites could not look at it (vv. 7–8). But that glory was fading (katargoumenon — being brought to an end, phased out). If even the ministry of condemnation came with such glory, how much more glorious is the ministry that brings righteousness (vv. 9–11)? What once had glory now has none in comparison, as a lamp has none at sunrise; and what was being brought to an end is set against what is permanent.

Because that hope is permanent, Paul says, he is very bold (v. 12) — parrēsia, the freedom to speak everything with nothing concealed, which is the opposite of managing an impression. The veil over Moses’s face (v. 13; Ex. 34:29–35) then becomes a powerful theological symbol. Moses put the veil on so that the Israelites could not see the glory fading — its end was hidden. Paul then makes a startling hermeneutical claim (vv. 14–15): the same veil lies over the hearts of those who read the old covenant without Christ. They read the words but the light is blocked; they read Moses but cannot see that he was pointing to Christ. When a person turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (v. 16) — and the glory they see is not merely the fading glory of Sinai but the unfading, surpassing glory of Christ.

Verse 17 draws the consequence: the Lord and the Spirit are one in this work, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom — not licence, but release from a covenant that could only condemn, and from the exhausting business of maintaining the veil.

The chapter climaxes in one of the most luminous sentences in the New Testament (v. 18): “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.” Transformation comes by beholding. The unveiled face gazing at the Lord’s glory is itself being changed into that glory — not all at once but progressively, degree by degree. This is sanctification: not primarily effort but gaze; not primarily discipline but encounter with glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Moses passage (Ex. 34) in Paul’s reading makes a claim that has been debated since the patristic period: Paul appears to say that Moses wore the veil to prevent the Israelites from seeing the glory’s end (to telos tou katargoumenou, v. 13), whereas Exodus says he wore it because the Israelites were afraid of his shining face. Paul is reading the text through the lens of its fulfilment in Christ: the entire Mosaic economy was a temporary arrangement pointing beyond itself, and the veil that covered Moses’s face symbolises the veil that covers the hearts of those who read him without recognising his Christological pointing.

The transformation passage (v. 18) is the key text for the Reformed understanding of sanctification as a work of the Spirit through the Word. Beholding — katoptrizomenoi (gazing as in a mirror, or reflecting as a mirror) — is the mechanism. The Word presents Christ; the Spirit uses the Word to produce in the believer the image they behold. John Owen, commenting on this verse, says that the primary means of sanctification is not moral effort but contemplation of the glory of Christ as revealed in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: A spiritual director works with a young Christian who is exhausted by the effort of sanctification — constantly striving, measuring, failing, striving again. She introduces him to the practice of deliberate meditation on specific passages that describe the character and glory of Christ, asking him to rest in the image rather than immediately applying it. After several months he reports something shifting in his desires and responses — not through effort but through what this verse would call beholding. The transformation is from the Lord who is the Spirit; the means is the unveiled face gazing at glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?

Paul now runs an argument he will repeat three times in five verses, and its form is always the same: if the lesser thing had that much glory, think what the greater must have.

First, the phrase that startles: the ministry of death. Applied to the law given at Sinai by God himself, it sounds close to blasphemy. But Paul has just explained it. The commandment is good; what it does to a sinner is fatal, because it can only ever tell him what he has failed to be. He is not disparaging the law. He is describing its effect on people like us.

Now stage the scene behind the verse, because everything depends on it. Moses has been forty days on the mountain. He comes down carrying the tablets, and he does not know that his face is shining (Ex. 34:29). Aaron and the people see him and are afraid to come near. The light is not his; it is residue. He has been standing in the presence of God and has come away carrying some of it on his skin, the way a man who has been near a fire comes back smelling of smoke.

And it was so bright that they could not look at him. Note that carefully, because it is Paul’s whole point. That is the glory of the covenant that kills. That is the brightness attached to the ministry that could only condemn.

Then the phrase he slips in almost quietly: which was being brought to an end. The shine on Moses’ face was fading even while they were too frightened to look at it. It was real glory, and it was temporary, and both things were true at once.

So the question in verse 8 answers itself. If a fading light on one man’s face after forty days on a mountain was more than a nation could look at, what is the weight of the ministry that does not condemn but makes righteous, that does not sit on the skin but is written on the heart, and that does not fade?

There is something here for the Christian who reads the Old Testament and feels quietly short-changed. The fire on the mountain, the sea opening, the pillar of cloud, the shining face — it can seem that they got the spectacle and we got the routine of an ordinary Tuesday. Paul says the comparison is real and runs entirely the other way. They had a glory nobody could look at, and it was on its way out. You have a glory that does not fade, in a covenant that cannot be broken, administered by the Spirit of God living inside ordinary people. The reason it looks less impressive is that it has moved inside, where the work needed doing.

And there is one more thing in the picture. The face that shone on Sinai was a borrowed light on a mortal man, and it went out. Centuries later three men watched another face on another mountain, and his face shone like the sun (Matt. 17:2) — and that light was not residue from a visit. It was his own, coming out. Moses was there to see it, and this time the glory belonged to the man in the middle.

verseByVerse.quote: For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.

Three verses, and Paul is pressing the same comparison from three directions: what the two ministries do, how they compare when set side by side, and how long each one lasts.

First, what they do. One is the ministry of condemnation, the other of righteousness. Both words are courtroom words. The law brings a verdict of guilty, and brings it accurately. The gospel brings a verdict of righteous, and brings it to the same defendant. That is the whole distance between Sinai and Calvary in two nouns.

Then the strange sentence in verse 10: what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. Paul is not contradicting himself. He is describing what happens when a real light is put beside a greater one. Anyone who has watched a lamp left burning as the sun comes up has seen it. The lamp has not changed and it was never a fraud; it is simply that, in the new light, there is nothing left for it to do.

And in verse 11 the decisive difference: one was being brought to an end, the other is permanent. The word for permanent means abiding, remaining, staying put. The old arrangement was always scaffolding — good work, necessary work, and put up around a building that was coming.

This matters practically for how a Christian reads the first three-quarters of his Bible. It would be easy to conclude from this passage that the Old Testament has been superseded and can be quietly shelved. Paul, who is about to say that the Israelites read Moses with a veil on, is not saying that. He quotes the Old Testament constantly, including in this very argument; his point is not that the old covenant was wrong but that it was never meant to be the end. The scaffolding does not become rubbish when the building appears. It becomes the thing that shows you how the building went up.

There is also a warning in the fading, aimed at us rather than at Israel. Glory that fades is not only a feature of the old covenant; it is the feature of everything else you might build a life on. Health fades. Beauty fades famously and fast. Careers end, reputations get revised, the house is sold to strangers, and the achievements that took twenty years are summarised in one line at a funeral. None of these things is worthless — the shine on Moses’ face was real. They are simply all being brought to an end, and the only question that matters is whether you have anything that is not.

Here is a way to test what you are actually resting on. Take whatever you would find hardest to lose and ask one question of it: in a hundred years, will it still be there? Almost nothing survives that question. What Paul is holding out is the one ministry that does — a covenant that will not be revised, a righteousness that will not be reviewed, a glory with no expiry attached to it. Set beside that, the brightest thing this world can put on a face is a lamp at sunrise.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.

The boldness comes first, and notice where it comes from. Not from temperament — Paul has just told us he was too anxious to preach at Troas. Not from success. Since we have such a hope. The confidence is a conclusion drawn from what he has been describing: a glory that does not fade, a covenant that will not be withdrawn.

The word is parrēsia, and its root meaning is freedom of speech — the right of a citizen to say everything, to speak without concealment. It is the opposite of the guarded half-sentence. Paul has nothing to manage and nothing to hide, so he can say it all.

Then a comparison that has puzzled readers since the early centuries, and it should be handled honestly rather than smoothed over. Exodus 34 says Moses veiled his face because the people were afraid of it. Paul says he veiled it so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end — that is, so they would not watch the glory dying away.

Is Paul rewriting Exodus? No, and it is worth seeing what he is actually doing. Exodus records what happened; Paul is reading it in the light of what it turned out to mean. The narrative gives the reason at the time — fear — and Paul, standing on the far side of the cross, sees the significance the veil carried in the whole arrangement: an old covenant whose glory was never permanent, and whose end was screened from the people living under it. This is not allegory imposed on the text. It is the same instinct the Lord himself modelled on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets to interpret what was said about himself (Lk. 24:27).

But sit with the pastoral picture in it, because it is very human. Moses is covering something that is fading. He is managing an impression. However tender the motive — and it was tender — the effect is that the people are dealing with a screen rather than a face.

That instinct is not confined to prophets. It is one of the most common conditions of religious life. Something has gone quiet inside — the love has cooled, the prayers have dried up, the certainty has thinned — and rather than say so, we put on the veil. We answer fine. We keep the vocabulary, the attendance, the tone of voice. And it works, which is the trouble; nobody can see a fading glory through a cloth, so nobody ever asks.

Paul’s alternative is not to shine harder. It is boldness — the open face of a man whose glory is not his own and is therefore not running out. That is why he can afford to be seen. The person whose light is borrowed and fading must manage how much of himself is visible. The person who has been given a glory that does not fade has no reason to cover anything, including his weakness. Paul will spend four chapters telling this church about his failures precisely because he has nothing left to protect.

verseByVerse.quote: But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.

The veil moves. It was on Moses’ face; now it is over the reader’s heart. And Paul says something painful about his own people: that the Scriptures they revere are being read in the synagogue every Sabbath by minds that have been hardened to what they are for.

Two things must be said before anything else, because this passage has been misused with terrible consequences. First, Paul is not writing as an outsider. He is a Jew — a Hebrew of Hebrews — who says elsewhere that he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish in his heart for his kinsmen, and could wish himself accursed for their sake (Rom. 9:2–3). This is not contempt. It is grief. Second, he does not treat the hardening as final. Within a couple of sentences he will say that the veil is removed whenever a person turns — a present possibility, open now, and he himself is the standing proof that it happens to the hardest cases.

Now the substance. The veil is not over the text; the text is fine. It is over the heart. The words are read accurately, translated correctly, memorised, honoured — and the thing they were written to point at is not seen. That is what makes this so serious. The problem was never a lack of Bible.

Which brings the passage uncomfortably close to home, and it should be allowed to. Christian readers can do exactly the same thing. It is entirely possible to read the Bible through with a plan, to know the names and the dates and the outline of every book, and to have missed the person the whole library was assembled to present. Sacrifices become ancient customs rather than a picture of what it costs to deal with sin. The exodus becomes national history rather than the pattern of every rescue God performs. Reading Scripture without seeing Christ in it is not a Jewish failing. It is a human one, and any of us can do it in English.

There is also a hard truth here about what conviction cannot achieve. The veil is not removed by argument. Paul, of all people, could out-argue any man in a synagogue, and he does not say here that the answer is a better case. He says the veil is taken away only through Christ. That is worth knowing if you are the one praying for a relative who knows all the answers and remains cold. You are not up against a shortage of information.

And it is worth knowing what did happen to Paul on the Damascus road. He did not lose an argument. He was struck blind, and then something like scales fell from his eyes (Acts 9:18) — the veil removed by the one person who can remove it, in a man who had been furiously certain he was reading Moses correctly. Nobody is beyond that. Not the relative you have given up on, and not the version of yourself that has been reading these pages for years without seeing anything.

verseByVerse.quote: But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.

Eight words, and they are the hinge of the chapter.

Paul is once more reaching back into Exodus 34. There is a detail in that chapter easily missed: Moses wore the veil among the people, but whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out (Ex. 34:34). The covering was for the crowd. In the presence of God it came off. Paul takes that habit of one man and makes it the pattern for anyone: turn to the Lord, and the veil comes off.

Notice the word turns. It is the ordinary word for turning round — a change of direction, not a change of opinion. This is what the Bible means by conversion, and the picture is deliberately physical. A man walking one way stops and walks the other. He does not add something to his life; he reverses.

Notice too what it does not say. It does not say the veil is removed when a person understands enough, or has read enough, or has been convinced by a sufficient weight of evidence. Nor does it say when a person has cleaned himself up first. It says when one turns. That is all. The turning is not the achievement that earns the sight; it is the moment the sight is given.

And it is passive: the veil is removed. Not he removes the veil. Nobody pulls the covering off his own heart, any more than a blind man cures himself by deciding to see. Something is done to him. This is the whole difference between religion and the gospel: one tells a man to lift the veil, the other tells him that when he turns he will find it has already been taken.

Which makes this the most practical verse in the chapter for anyone reading it from the outside — or from the inside on a cold morning. If the Bible has gone flat, if God has become an idea you defend rather than a person you know, the instruction is not try harder to feel it. It is turn. Stop, face the other way, and speak to him. Paul does not attach conditions to it. He does not say when one turns and has sorted himself out, or when one turns for the first time, or when one turns having not wasted the last ten years. The sentence is open at both ends.

And what a thing it is to say about God, that he is that easy to find. There is no antechamber, no delay, no preliminary examination, no queue. A man turns and the covering is gone, and he is looking straight at the Lord. That is what it cost the Son of God to arrange — the veil in the temple torn from the top down, on the afternoon he died, so that the way in would stand open for everyone who ever turned round (Matt. 27:51). Nobody has ever come and been told to wait.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

Two claims, tightly joined, and the second is one of the great sentences of the Christian life.

The first — the Lord is the Spirit — needs handling with care. Paul is not collapsing the persons of the Trinity into one, as though Christ and the Spirit were merely two names for the same person. He distinguishes them plainly enough elsewhere, and even in this verse he can speak of the Spirit of the Lord, which requires two. What he is saying is that in the passage he has been expounding, the Lord to whom a man turns and the Spirit who does the transforming are not rivals or alternatives. To turn to Christ is to come under the working of the Spirit. They are one in operation. You do not get the Son without the Spirit, or the Spirit without the Son.

Then the freedom. And the first question to ask is: freedom from what?

From the veil, in the first place — from reading the words of God with the meaning screened off. But the context has been building a bigger answer. Freedom from the covenant that could only condemn. From the standard that made demands and gave no power. From the terrible arithmetic of a religion in which everything depends on your performance and your performance is not good enough. And, given verse 13, freedom from the exhausting business of managing the veil — of maintaining an appearance while something quietly fades underneath.

What it is not is freedom to do as you please. Paul is emphatic elsewhere: you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh (Gal. 5:13). A man who defines liberty as the absence of all constraint has never looked honestly at what actually rules him. The heaviest masters people serve are not laws imposed from outside; they are appetites, resentments and fears that were chosen freely and cannot now be put down.

Christian freedom is more like the freedom of a musician than the freedom of a man with no commitments. Years under a discipline he did not invent produce someone who can finally play what he hears. He is not free from the instrument. He is free on it.

So run the test on yourself. Where is the pressure in your religion? If you obey God mainly to keep something bad from happening — his disappointment, his withdrawal, the sense that you are behind — then whatever you have, the atmosphere of it is not freedom. Something in you is still standing at the foot of Sinai. The mark of the new covenant is not that the commandments have gone soft. It is that the fear has gone out of them, because the verdict was settled before you began.

That is what the Spirit does where he is. He does not merely help a slave work harder. He makes the slave a son, and then teaches him to say Father (Rom. 8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

The chapter has been climbing since verse 7, and here it arrives. Nearly every word is load-bearing, so take them one at a time.

We all. On Sinai it was one man, and the nation stood at the bottom of the mountain and was warned not to touch it. Now the whole congregation is on the mountain. There is no spiritual class in the new covenant who see what ordinary members do not. The tired mother, the apprentice, the man who has never been asked to do anything in church — we all.

With unveiled face. The covering has been taken off. Nothing stands between the believer and the glory of God; the face is bare and it is safe for it to be bare, which is more than Moses could say.

Beholding. The Greek word can mean gazing into a mirror or reflecting like one, and scholars have argued about it for centuries. The context of Moses looking at God’s glory favours gazing, and the mirror image is worth keeping in mind: we do not see him yet as he is, but truly, in the gospel, as in a good mirror. Either way the posture is the same. It is looking.

Are being transformed. The verb is metamorphoumetha — the word used of the Lord’s own transfiguration. It is passive: this is being done to us. And it is in the present continuous: it is happening now, in the ordinary weeks, whether or not it can be felt.

From one degree of glory to another. By stages. Nobody arrives in a morning.

Now put it together, because the practical claim is startling and most of us do not live as though we believed it. We become what we look at. Sanctification, in this verse, is not first a matter of effort, resolutions or accountability, useful as those are. It is a matter of gaze. The transformation is a side-effect of contemplation — which is why John Owen spent his life arguing that the great means of holiness is the beholding of the glory of Christ, and why a man can white-knuckle his way through a list of disciplines for a decade and change very little.

The principle holds in the other direction too, which is where it becomes uncomfortable. Whatever you gaze at is forming you. Look for two hours every evening at people who are richer, and you will become discontented; you will not have decided to. Feed on outrage and you will become an angry person. The mechanism does not care what is in front of it.

So the question is not really am I trying hard enough? It is what am I looking at? Add up the hours honestly. Then ask where in the week Christ is actually put in front of you long enough for anything to happen — not read about, but looked at.

And notice how the sentence ends, because it takes the whole weight off the one doing the looking: this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit. The change is not manufactured by the intensity of your concentration. He is the one doing it, and he has never abandoned a half-finished work. From one degree to another, in people who mostly cannot see it happening, he is quietly making his own likeness — until the day the mirror is taken away, and we shall see him as he is, and being like him will no longer be a process but a fact (1 Jn. 3:2).
